STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY The review was prospectively registered in PROSPERO and used a comprehensive, predefined search strategy across ten international and Chinese databases. Study selection, data extraction and methodological quality appraisal were conducted independently by two reviewers using the 2016 Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. A JBI meta-aggregation approach was applied to systematically extract, categorise and synthesise qualitative findings from the 15 included studies. Restricting inclusion to studies published in Chinese or English, and excluding records for which full texts could not be obtained, may have introduced language and publication bias. Heterogeneity in participants’ characteristics, healthcare systems and cultural contexts across countries may limit the transferability and generalisability of the synthesised findings. Introduction Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common chronic respiratory disease characterised by persistent airflow limitation and progressive decline in lung function. It is associated with high incidence, substantial mortality, a prolonged disease course, difficulty of cure and frequent exacerbations, posing a serious threat to patients’ lives and placing a heavy burden on families and healthcare systems. 1 The number of patients with COPD worldwide has reached nearly 100 million. Among adults over 40 years of age in China, the prevalence of COPD is as high as 13.6% and continues to increase. 2 It is predicted that by 2030, COPD will become the third leading cause of death globally. 3 These figures highlight the urgent need to strengthen comprehensive prevention, treatment and long-term management of COPD. Increasing evidence suggests that effective COPD control depends not only on pharmacological treatment but also on patients’ capacity to engage in sustained self-management. Educational interventions that enhance self-care agency and rational drug use have been shown to improve patients’ ability to participate in disease control, 4 while broader self-management programmes can reduce symptom burden, decrease hospitalisation frequency and improve quality of life. 5 Such self-management requires close cooperation between patients, families, communities and medical professionals to control disease symptoms, cope with physical and psychological impacts and adjust lifestyle to meet the challenges of long-term chronic illness. 6 However, qualitative and quantitative studies indicate that, in practice, patients often encounter substantial barriers to self-management, including limited disease knowledge, insufficient social support, negative emotions such as anxiety and depression and various technical and resource constraints. 6 7 In recent years, qualitative research exploring the self-management experiences and needs of patients with COPD has gradually increased, providing rich insights into how individuals perceive and manage their condition in different cultural and healthcare contexts. 6 7 Nevertheless, single qualitative studies usually focus on specific settings or subgroups and therefore cannot comprehensively and deeply reflect broader patterns in patients’ inner feelings, challenges and support needs. To address this gap, the present study conducts a qualitative systematic review and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) meta-aggregation of existing qualitative research on COPD self-management. Our aim is to systematically synthesise patients’ real experiences, problems and needs in the self-management process, thereby generating evidence to inform the design and implementation of more precise and effective self-management interventions and to support patients in actively adapting to their condition and improving their quality of life. Methods Design This qualitative systematic review was prospectively registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number CRD42024607051). The conduct and reporting of the review followed the Enhancing Transparency in Reporting the Synthesis of Qualitative Research (ENTREQ) statement. 8 The review was conducted using the JBI meta-aggregation approach for qualitative evidence synthesis. The completed ENTREQ checklist for this review is provided in ( online supplemental file S1 ) Patient and public involvement Patients and/or the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of this research. Inclusion and exclusion criteria of the literature This study adheres to the PICoS principle for inclusion criteria. The following are the listed inclusion criteria: (1) Participants: patients with a clear diagnosis of COPD, aged ≥18 years; (2) Phenomena of interest: the real feelings, experiences and needs of patients with COPD during the self-management process; (3) Context: the process of self-management and rehabilitation of patients in medical institutions, communities or at home; and (4) Study type: qualitative research, including ethnography, phenomenology, grounded theory and other qualitative designs. For mixed-population studies (eg, studies including patients with COPD and other chronic respiratory diseases), we included the study only if data for patients with COPD could be clearly distinguished and extracted separately; otherwise such studies were excluded. For mixed-methods studies, we included articles when the qualitative component focusing on COPD self-management could be identified and analysed independently. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) literature that could not be obtained in full text or had incomplete data, despite attempts to obtain the full text through institutional subscriptions, interlibrary loan and, where appropriate, by contacting the authors; (2) repetitively published literature (in which case the most complete or recent report was retained); and (3) studies not published in Chinese or English. Literature search strategy A systematic search was conducted in ten electronic databases: PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, Embase, CNKI, Wanfang Database, VIP Database and CBM, from database inception to March 2025. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) or equivalent controlled vocabulary with free-text terms related to “chronic obstructive pulmonary disease”, “self-management”, “self-care”, “experience”, “perception”, “needs” and “qualitative research”, using Boolean operators and truncation as appropriate for each database. The search strategies were adapted to the syntax and indexing of each database (eg, using MeSH terms in PubMed and Emtree terms in Embase), and, where applicable, filters for humans and adults (≥18 years) were applied. No restrictions were placed on publication year, but only studies published in Chinese or English were considered. An example of the search strategy for PubMed is shown in online supplemental S1 figure . The full, precise search strategies for all databases, including field tags, operators, limits and filters, are provided in online supplemental file S2 . Literature screening and data extraction Two researchers (both having received training in evidence-based nursing) independently screened the literature and conducted cross-checks. After removing duplicate records using EndNote V.21 software, they first read the titles and abstracts to exclude obviously irrelevant studies, then assessed the full texts to determine final eligibility. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third researcher. Data were extracted using a standardised form. The extracted information included study characteristics (first author, publication year, country, study design, data collection methods, setting and participant characteristics), the phenomena of interest (experiences and needs related to COPD self-management) and qualitative findings relevant to self-management (participants’ quotations and authors’ interpretive statements). These qualitative findings formed the units of analysis for the subsequent meta-aggregation. Evaluation of methodological quality of literature Two researchers independently evaluated the quality of the literature based on the 2016 version of the JBI Quality Evaluation Criteria for Qualitative Research in Evidence-Based Health Care. Each of the 10 evaluation items was evaluated with ‘Yes’, ‘No’, ‘Unclear’ or ‘Not Applicable’. The quality of the literature was classified into three levels: A level for complete compliance, B level for partial compliance and C level for complete non-compliance. In case of disagreement in the evaluation results, the third researcher participated in the discussion and the literature with quality grades of A and B was finally included. Literature analysis method We synthesised the qualitative evidence using the JBI meta-aggregation approach. 9 10 In this approach, each extracted finding (participant quotation and/or author interpretation relevant to COPD self-management) was treated as a unit of meaning and assigned a level of credibility. Following the guidance of Lockwood et al 10 , conceptually similar findings were grouped into categories and these categories were then further aggregated into overarching synthesised findings that captured core meanings across the studies while remaining close to the original data. Two reviewers independently coded the extracted findings and developed the initial categories. A third reviewer then reviewed and refined the coding framework and the grouping of categories into synthesised findings. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached. This iterative process enhanced the transparency and rigour of the qualitative synthesis. Results Literature search results The study selection process is summarised in the flow diagram shown in online supplemental S2 figure . The initial search yielded 2474 records. After removal of duplicates, 1628 records remained for screening. Of these, 58 articles were retained based on title and abstract screening, and following full-text assessment, re-screening and quality appraisal, 15 qualitative studies were finally included in the synthesis. 11 , 25 These comprised 3 studies published in Chinese 12 21 24 and 12 in English. 1113 , 20 22 23 25 Basic characteristics and quality evaluation results of included literature The basic characteristics of the included studies are summarised in online supplemental table S1 . The 15 studies 11 , 25 involved a total of 251 patients with COPD. These studies included 1 descriptive qualitative study, 18 4 grounded theory studies 11 20 22 25 and 10 phenomenological studies. 12 , 1719 21 23 24 Across the 15 included studies, 52 individual findings were identified. Their synthesis is presented in Synthesised findings from the meta-aggregation. The extraction results and quality evaluation results of the literature are presented in online supplemental table S2 . Synthesised findings from the meta-aggregation Across the included studies, 52 findings were identified and grouped into 13 categories, which were further synthesised into 4 overarching synthesised findings. To improve clarity and avoid a list-like presentation, the findings are presented below as an interpretive narrative supported by selected illustrative quotations, rather than as a comprehensive listing of quotations for every individual point. Synthesised finding 1: physical symptom burden strongly shapes psychological well-being during COPD self-management Across the included studies, patients consistently described a close and often reciprocal relationship between physical symptom burden and psychological well-being during COPD self-management. Breathlessness, fatigue, sleep disturbance, reduced exercise tolerance and progressive functional decline were widely reported and frequently triggered fear, frustration, sadness and helplessness. For many patients, these symptoms not only limited physical functioning but also undermined social participation, confidence and emotional stability. However, psychological responses were not entirely uniform. While distress predominated, a minority of participants described gradual acceptance, adaptation and a more hopeful outlook over time, indicating heterogeneity in coping across individuals and care contexts. Category 1: physical symptom burden and disruption of daily life Progressive physical decline was described across almost all included studies as a central challenge to self-management. Patients frequently reported that dyspnoea, fatigue, low energy levels, sleep problems and recurrent exacerbations disrupted routine activities and reduced their ability to maintain independence in daily life. These symptoms often affected not only self-care but also family roles, mobility and participation in previously valued social activities. Some accounts also suggested that worsening symptoms created a sense of unpredictability, making patients hesitant to plan ahead or leave the home. One participant captured this loss vividly: “I used to love dancing… Now I can’t even finish a song”. 22 Although symptom burden was widespread, its impact appeared more severe among patients with advanced disease and among those living in settings where supportive resources were limited. Category 2: diverse and evolving psychological responses to chronic illness Patients described a broad range of emotional responses to living with COPD, although fear, anxiety, frustration and hopelessness were more commonly reported than emotional acceptance. Psychological distress was often linked to the experience of breathlessness, uncertainty about disease progression, fear of exacerbation, loss of autonomy and the cumulative burden of long-term illness. For some, these feelings were intensified by worries about becoming dependent on others or about being unable to fulfil family and social responsibilities. Others responded by minimising symptoms or avoiding engagement with treatment, suggesting that emotional distress could also shape behavioural patterns in self-management. One participant remarked, “I wake up at night struggling to breathe—it’s terrifying when you can’t get air”. 18 At the same time, a smaller number of participants described greater optimism and acceptance, often in the presence of family encouragement or trust in professional care, indicating that psychological adaptation existed along a continuum rather than following a single fixed pattern. Synthesised finding 2: patients face multiple and interrelated barriers to effective self-management Most studies showed that patients encountered several overlapping barriers in understanding, sustaining and integrating COPD self-management into everyday life. These barriers included limited disease knowledge, difficulty adapting to long-term behavioural change, poor adherence to recommended regimens, financial strain and restricted access to healthcare services. Rather than occurring in isolation, such challenges often reinforced one another. For example, inadequate knowledge could reduce confidence, which in turn affected adherence, while financial difficulties and limited service access could further constrain patients’ capacity to manage symptoms effectively. Although these problems were reported across settings, structural barriers were more prominent in rural or low-resource contexts, whereas patients in better-resourced settings more often emphasised uncertainty, stigma and the hidden burden of chronic illness. Category 3: inadequate disease knowledge and self-management skills Insufficient knowledge about COPD and its management was evident in almost all included studies. Patients reported uncertainty about symptom monitoring, exacerbation management, medication use, inhaler techniques, home oxygen therapy, smoking-related risks and pulmonary rehabilitation. These knowledge deficits reduced confidence in decision-making and often left patients unsure how to respond when symptoms worsened. In several studies, participants also felt that information from professionals was incomplete, delayed or difficult to understand, which further limited their ability to manage the disease effectively. One participant explained, “No one ever asks if I need information—they just say, ‘You have COPD, figure it out’”. 22 Such gaps were especially apparent among older adults and those with lower educational levels, whereas patients who had received structured education tended to describe greater understanding and confidence. Category 4: difficulties adapting to lifestyle change and sustaining adherence Many patients described difficulty adapting to the behavioural and lifestyle changes required for long-term COPD management. These difficulties were reflected in continued smoking, low motivation for rehabilitation or exercise, reluctance to use medicines as prescribed and a tendency to delay active management until symptoms became severe. In some studies, poor adaptation was also linked to altered self-identity, reduced confidence and a sense of diminished capability, which made it harder for patients to incorporate self-management into everyday routines. Adherence problems therefore appeared to be shaped not only by knowledge deficits, but also by emotional resistance and the burden of ongoing lifestyle adjustment. One participant stated, “I’m just a disabled person now—incapable of anything”, 23 reflecting the low self-efficacy that often accompanied poor adjustment. Although these barriers were common, some participants gradually renegotiated their roles and routines over time, suggesting variation in how self-management was incorporated into daily life. Category 5: financial strain and limitations in healthcare access This category reflects the concrete economic and service-related barriers that patients were already experiencing in daily self-management. Across several studies, the costs of medication, oxygen equipment, consultations and long-term treatment led some patients to reduce dosages, interrupt treatment or delay care. In addition to direct medical costs, some patients also described the wider material consequences of chronic illness, including pressure on household finances and difficulty accessing appropriate services because of distance, mobility limitations or shortages in local provision. Limited access to specialist care, pulmonary rehabilitation and chronic disease support programmes further weakened patients’ capacity to manage COPD effectively, especially in rural or resource-constrained areas. One participant noted, “This medication requires twice daily, but I use it once—it’s too expensive”. 17 These accounts indicate that financial hardship and inadequate service availability functioned as immediate barriers to self-management rather than merely perceived future concerns. Category 6: dual influences of religious beliefs and cultural practices Religious beliefs and cultural practices had both supportive and constraining effects on COPD self-management. In some studies, spiritual beliefs provided comfort, hope and a sense of meaning that helped patients endure chronic symptoms and maintain motivation. In other cases, however, cultural practices or traditional remedies conflicted with medical recommendations and were associated with delayed treatment, reduced adherence or worsening symptoms. Some patients appeared to move flexibly between biomedical advice and culturally rooted practices, while others relied more heavily on non-medical coping approaches. One participant reported, “During Ramadan, I abstain completely”, 14 illustrating how cultural practices could directly affect self-management behaviours. Overall, these influences were context-dependent and varied across cultural and religious settings, highlighting the need for culturally sensitive support. Synthesised finding 3: some patients develop active coping strategies and self-management resources The included studies also showed that a proportion of patients developed practical and adaptive ways of managing COPD in daily life. These strategies included monitoring symptoms, adjusting activity levels, learning disease-management skills, maintaining a positive outlook and drawing on support from multiple sources. For these patients, self-management was not only a response to illness but also an active process of learning, experimentation and adjustment. However, such approaches were not universal. Some patients remained reliant on reactive, limited or avoidant forms of management, indicating marked variation in self-management capacity and resilience across the included studies. Category 7: self-regulation strategies for symptom control Many patients described practical strategies for reducing symptoms and preventing exacerbations. These included avoiding environmental triggers, pacing activities, monitoring bodily changes, practising breathing or sputum-clearance techniques, participating in rehabilitation and keeping medicines readily available. In some cases, patients also developed highly individualised routines based on prior experience of symptom fluctuation, which helped them feel more in control of daily management. At the same time, the quality and sophistication of these strategies varied, with some approaches appearing more flexible and effective than others. One participant explained, “I track my symptoms, control my activities and diet, and assess disease stability without relying solely on healthcare providers”. 19 Although self-regulation strategies were widely described, some patients relied mainly on short-term avoidance or energy-conservation patterns that could help temporarily but also risked reinforcing deconditioning and social isolation. Category 8: positive reframing and psychological adaptation A minority of participants described developing greater emotional resilience over time. These patients reframed COPD as a condition to be managed rather than as a purely catastrophic event, and they emphasised hope, acceptance and confidence in ongoing self-management. Positive adaptation was often associated with a gradual process of adjusting expectations, recognising small improvements and focusing on what could still be controlled in daily life. Some patients also appeared to draw strength from supportive relationships or from prior experiences of coping with adversity. As one participant stated, “We must learn to coexist with COPD without surrendering, maintaining hope”. 16 Although such positive reframing was not universal, it suggests that psychological adaptation may function as an important internal resource for sustaining self-management over time. Category 9: active mobilisation of support from multiple sources This category reflects patients’ active efforts to seek and mobilise support from different sources in order to manage COPD more effectively. Participants described asking healthcare professionals for advice, searching for information, learning from peers and making use of practical help from family members or institutions. In this sense, support was not only something received passively, but also something patients actively pursued when they recognised limits in their own knowledge or capacity. Such efforts could strengthen confidence, improve access to information and make disease management feel less isolating. One participant stated, “If I don’t speak up, how can clinicians help me?”. 17 These active help-seeking behaviours were more frequently reported in urban or better-resourced settings, whereas patients in more isolated or resource-constrained environments often described fewer opportunities to access diversified sources of support. Synthesised finding 4: patients express multidimensional and continuing support needs Across almost all studies, patients articulated support needs that extended well beyond medication alone. These included clearer and more accessible information, sustained professional guidance, stronger financial and social protection and greater emotional support from family members, peers and healthcare professionals. Rather than being isolated requests, these needs were often interrelated and reflected patients’ attempts to cope with the long-term burden of living with COPD in everyday life. Although these needs were widely shared, their specific forms varied across healthcare systems, social contexts, family structures and levels of available community support. Category 10: need for accessible and practical disease information Nearly all patients expressed a strong need for clearer, more practical and more timely information about COPD, including symptom management, treatment options, disease progression and daily self-care. Many also preferred information to be delivered through multiple formats, such as written materials, videos or repeated explanations, rather than through one-off verbal instruction. Patients’ accounts suggested that information was valued not only for knowledge itself, but also for the reassurance and sense of control it could provide. One participant commented, “Knowing the truth about the disease is crucial”. 16 Although the desire for information was nearly universal, preferences regarding timing, format and depth of education varied between individuals and some patients reported feeling overwhelmed by technical or inconsistent explanations. Category 11: need for ongoing professional and personalised rehabilitation support Patients commonly reported needing more individualised and continuous professional support than they were currently receiving. This included clearer rehabilitation instructions, tailored exercise guidance, assistance with comorbidity management, better communication with clinicians and regular follow-up after discharge. Several studies also suggested that patients valued professional support that took account of their personal circumstances, symptom burden and changing capabilities rather than relying solely on standardised advice. As one participant explained, “Without clear rehab instructions, I can’t persist—experts should explain its benefits”. 13 Overall, participants described a gap between their need for ongoing, person-centred support and the episodic, standardised care that they often experienced in practice. Category 12: need for stronger financial and social support In contrast to Category 5, which describes barriers already experienced in everyday management, this category captures patients’ expectations for stronger long-term financial protection and broader social support. Participants expressed the need for improved insurance coverage, reduced treatment costs, community-based services, practical family assistance and opportunities to maintain social participation despite COPD. In many accounts, support needs extended beyond symptom control to preserving meaningful social roles, maintaining dignity and continuing valued family relationships. One participant stated, “I want to keep up with my grandchildren”, 22 showing that support needs were closely connected to everyday life and social belonging. Although these needs were described across settings, some patients focused more on informal family support, whereas others emphasised formal welfare measures and community resources, reflecting variation in healthcare systems and social expectations. Category 13: need for emotional and psychological support Unlike Category 9, which concerns patients’ active efforts to seek support, this category focuses on patients’ unmet need for empathy, reassurance and emotionally supportive relationships. Many accounts reflected loneliness, fear and a sense of being insufficiently understood, particularly when symptoms were severe or support networks were weak. Patients often valued not only practical assistance but also the experience of being listened to, accompanied and emotionally acknowledged by family members, peers or healthcare professionals. One participant said, “To doctors, I’m just another patient—a nurse’s companionship would mean so much”. 17 Structured psychological interventions and organised peer-support services were mentioned only rarely, suggesting an important gap between patients’ emotional needs and the support currently available. Discussion Addressing challenges in COPD self-management and enhancing comprehensive support This study showed that patients with COPD face multiple and interrelated barriers during self-management, including physiological limitations (eg, dyspnoea, fatigue, restricted mobility), psychological distress (eg, anxiety, depression stemming from insufficient disease knowledge and treatment uncertainty) and social isolation—reported in most included studies—exacerbating helplessness. These factors collectively contribute to poor self-management behaviours, aligning with prior research. 6 26 27 Potential causes include high disease burden, inadequate self-management awareness and insufficient social and professional guidance. 28 Domestic studies, such as Zhao et al , 29 demonstrated that COPD pulmonary rehabilitation programmes based on the IMB model effectively alleviate dyspnoea, improve exercise tolerance, enhance quality of life and boost adherence and self-management capacity. International research by Benzo and McEvoy 30 also highlighted that nurse-led motivational interviewing improves patient self-management. 31 Therefore, healthcare providers should use multidimensional, standardised and intelligent assessment tools to evaluate patients’ physical and mental states accurately, implement targeted interventions and foster confidence in self-management. Collaborative efforts among patients, families, clinicians and society are essential to provide holistic support—educational, emotional, financial and social—to mitigate the disease’s impact. Strengthening positive self-management behaviours to promote adaptation This study identified that COPD self-management behaviours are influenced by socioeconomic status, education level, health beliefs, social support, disease severity and psychological state, consistent with Sami et al . 28 Proactive patients exhibited adaptive strategies such as information-seeking, self-monitoring and skill acquisition. 24 Successful self-management experiences reinforce confidence, creating a positive reinforcing cycle of symptom recognition, medication adherence and physical activity. 18 Clinicians should adopt a holistic approach, acknowledging both challenges and achievements. 32 Such strategies encourage continuous adaptation and growth in disease management. Identifying multidimensional needs and reducing self-management burden Effective COPD self-management requires personalised support systems integrating familial, clinical, institutional and societal resources. 29 33 However, unmet needs persist, including knowledge gaps, inaccessible resources and mismatched services. Clinicians must prioritise patient-centred care by understanding individual preferences and providing continuous feedback. Personalised strategies should address physical rehabilitation, psychological adaptation and social integration. Internet-based platforms 34 could optimise remote monitoring and follow-up, 35 while family workshops and self-management diaries strengthen long-term adherence. 36 Pendoni et al 37 emphasised that robust social support systems enhance access to healthcare resources, disease education and emotional reinforcement, ultimately improving prognosis. 31 38 Governments, institutions and communities must collaborate to establish COPD support networks, improve resource accessibility and alleviate self-management burdens. Methodological considerations and limitations In interpreting these findings, several methodological limitations of the review should be considered. First, restricting inclusion to studies published in Chinese or English may have introduced language bias and reduced the global representativeness of the evidence. Second, despite attempts to obtain full texts through institutional access and interlibrary loan, three potentially relevant studies could not be retrieved and were therefore excluded, which may have resulted in the loss of additional qualitative insights. Third, the included studies differed in design, setting and participant characteristics (eg, age, disease severity and socioeconomic background), as well as in healthcare system and cultural context, which may have introduced heterogeneity and limited the transferability and generalisability of the synthesised findings. Finally, although the JBI meta-aggregation approach aims to remain close to the primary data, the processes of identifying, grouping and synthesising findings inevitably involve interpretive judgement by the review team. Strengths and limitations The review was prospectively registered in PROSPERO and used a comprehensive, predefined search strategy across 10 international and Chinese databases. Study selection, data extraction and methodological quality appraisal were conducted independently by two reviewers using the 2016 JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. A JBI meta-aggregation approach was applied to systematically extract, categorise and synthesise qualitative findings from the 15 included studies. Restricting inclusion to studies published in Chinese or English, and excluding records for which full texts could not be obtained, may have introduced language and publication bias. Heterogeneity in participants’ characteristics, healthcare systems and cultural contexts across countries may limit the transferability and generalisability of the synthesised findings. Conclusion This study systematically synthesised the lived experiences and unmet needs of patients with COPD in relation to self-management, highlighting important physical, psychological and social challenges, adaptive coping strategies and persistent gaps in support. The findings indicate that patients face multiple and interrelated barriers during self-management, underscoring the need for healthcare professionals to provide comprehensive guidance, reinforce proactive behaviours and strengthen patients’ self-management capacity. Clinicians should identify and address patients’ multidimensional needs through tailored and diversified support in order to reduce self-management burden and promote adaptation to chronic illness. These findings also suggest that stronger coordination across patient, family, community and clinical levels may help better address the multilevel needs identified in this review and improve quality of life for this population. documents.title: Virtual reality in adults with respiratory diseases experiencing dyspnoea: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Our aim was to evaluate virtual reality's effects in dyspnoea's management.
METHODS: Information sources: Trials were identified through a systematic search carried out on MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus and CINAHL until 17 March 2025.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Eligible studies were controlled trials including adults with dyspnoea associated with respiratory diseases, for whom virtual reality was implemented and compared with another intervention. Risk of bias: Risk of bias (ROB) was assessed using the ROB 2 tool.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: The primary outcome was dyspnoea. Secondary outcomes included exercise capacity, health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and muscle function. Effect size was expressed using standardised mean difference (SMD) or MD for primary and secondary outcomes, respectively (random-effects model). We used the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach to judge the certainty of evidence.
RESULTS: Included studies: 13 studies were selected, including 483 adults and using non-immersive tools (n=7) or immersive tools (n=6). Risk of bias in these studies was low (n=1), some concerns (n=8) and high risk (n=4).
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: No difference was found in dyspnoea (8 studies, 224 participants; SMD 0.02, 95% CI -0.82 to 0.86, I2=88.2%), exercise capacity (5 studies, 183 participants; MD 3.62, 95% CI -19.39 to 26.63, I2=39.8%) and in HRQOL (4 studies, 127 participants; MD -11.81, 95% CI -42.95 to 19.33, I2=98.9%). The data available were insufficient to conduct a pooled analysis for muscle function.
CONCLUSIONS: Limitations of evidence: The evidence is very uncertain about virtual reality's effects on dyspnoea due to risk of bias, imprecision and heterogeneity.
INTERPRETATION: Further studies are needed and should explore various aspects of the application of immersive virtual reality.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42023443280.

WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Respiratory diseases represent the main comorbidities associated with dyspnoea, a significant source of discomfort. Therefore, it appears imperative to offer treatments aimed at alleviating dyspnoea. An increasing number of studies are focusing on the use of virtual reality (VR) in respiratory diseases. A systematic review with meta-analysis was needed to evaluate the effects of VR on perceived dyspnoea. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS Screening across four databases identified 6624 reports. A total of 13 studies were included in this systematic review. No difference was found in dyspnoea (8 studies, 224 participants), exercise capacity (5 studies, 183 participants) and in health-related quality of life (4 studies, 127 participants). HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY Our confidence in effect estimates prevents us from drawing recommendations for the use of VR in clinical practice. This meta-analysis highlights the need to address several gaps in the use of VR: (1) more studies are needed, (2) multidimensional assessment tools for dyspnoea should be used and (3) multiple applications should be explored. Introduction Dyspnoea is defined as a subjective experience of breathing discomfort that may occur during exertion, even at low intensities or at rest. 1 Respiratory diseases represent the main comorbidities associated with this multidimensional symptom. 2 As a chronic manifestation, dyspnoea is a high-burden symptom. Chronic dyspnoea is defined as a persistent experience of breathing discomfort despite receiving the optimal treatment, leading to disability and deconditioning. 3 People suffering with chronic dyspnoea have been shown to have a significant increase in mortality, greater exercise limitation, impaired muscle function and a severe decline in activities of daily living and health-related quality of life (HRQOL). 4 Chronic dyspnoea is highly prevalent among individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), occurring in over 80% of cases, thereby making COPD the main cause of chronic dyspnoea. 2 5 In this context, the severity of dyspnoea generally increases with disease progression and during acute exacerbations. 6 Dyspnoea may also be acute and is a frequent reason for hospital admission. 7 It may occur de novo (eg, pneumoniae, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax) with, for instance, dyspnoea reported in 40%–90% of hospitalised patients with COVID-19 infection. 8 Alternatively, it may also manifest in the context of chronic dyspnoea (ie, acute-on-chronic). In this context, prevalence of dyspnoea exceeds 90% for people with acute exacerbation of COPD. 2 Finally, individuals experiencing severe dyspnoea at the onset of an acute respiratory condition may face challenges in recovering from this symptom. 9 10 Regardless of the condition, dyspnoea is a significant source of discomfort, and it therefore appears imperative to offer treatments aimed at alleviating dyspnoea. Among the most efficient rehabilitation treatments, exercise training is a key intervention and arguably the most fundamental one. 11 Exercise training has been demonstrated to alleviate dyspnoea and maintain HRQOL, while simultaneously enhancing exercise capacity. In addition, as is well documented, deconditioning and sarcopenia have been shown to have a significant impact on dyspnoea intensity. Conversely, exercise training has been demonstrated to result in substantial increases in muscle strength and mass. 11 However, the management of dyspnoea is challenging. Indeed, the expectation of dyspnoea may unfortunately be one of the primary barriers to participation in physical activity, thereby compromising the potential benefits of exercise. 12 Virtual reality (VR) is a technology that allows users to be immersed in a computer-generated environment, which can be fully immersive (via head-mounted displays) or non-immersive (delivered through standard screens). Immersive VR creates an illusory visual environment at the expense of the real physical world. 13 In contrast, non-immersive VR is typically two-dimensional and delivered through a computer or screen. 13 An increasing number of studies are focusing on the use of VR in respiratory diseases. 14 15 The hypotheses underlying the effects of VR on dyspnoea are numerous, with some manifesting from a single exposure and others requiring repeated exposure. For instance, Betka et al showed that participants with COVID-19 infection improved their persistent dyspnoea with a single VR exposure. 14 In this study, participants received VR at rest during which they observed an avatar in addition to synchronous feedback of their own breathing. This 5 min exposure suggested short-term effects, underpinned by multisensory integration. Distraction and emotional modulation are other short-term mechanisms which have been described after a single exposure. 14 16 Finally, with repeated exposure, the long-term effectiveness of VR in modulating dyspnoea may be linked to the sustained effects previously mentioned or, in the context of rehabilitation, to its ability to enhance self-efficacy, motivation and the enjoyment of physical activity, thereby promoting adherence to exercise. 17 Recent meta-analyses demonstrated that VR effectively improves both functional capacity and pulmonary function in people with COPD. However, these studies do not focus on dyspnoea, 18 19 neither acute nor chronic, 18 , 20 nor on quality of life. 18 , 20 Moreover, authors do not consider the potential impact of immersion levels or number of exposures on dyspnoea perception and management. Finally, while COPD is the primary respiratory disease associated with dyspnoea, other conditions, such as COVID-19, may also be impacted. Our objective was to evaluate the effects of VR on dyspnoea in adults with respiratory diseases. The secondary objectives were to evaluate the effect of VR on exercise capacity, muscle function and HRQOL in a population of individuals suffering from chronic breathlessness. Methods Protocol and registration This systematic review and meta-analysis followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, 21 was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023443280) and commenced on 13 July 2023. Eligibility criteria Studies including adults with acute or chronic respiratory conditions causing dyspnoea were eligible. To be considered, participants had to experience dyspnoea; in this context, studies had to assess dyspnoea, whether as an inclusion criterion, an outcome or a baseline measurement. All controlled interventional trials were included when VR (immersive and non-immersive) was implemented and compared with another intervention. The intervention settings, durations and frequencies were not restricted. We excluded studies that were (1) lacking sufficient detail on outcomes or the VR intervention, (2) not clearly measuring dyspnoea and (3) using a no-intervention control group. Full details of our eligibility criteria are available in online supplemental material 1 . Information sources Databases screened were MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus and CINAHL. We conducted a systematic search in databases from their creation to 17 March 2025. Search strategy Our search equation was built around Cochrane’s recommendations 22 specifying: (1) the population (eg, “Respiratory disease”), (2) the intervention (eg, “Virtual Reality”) and (3) the study design. These three components were constructed using Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms (or their equivalent) and free-text keywords and combined using the corresponding boolean operators. The full search strategy was detailed in online supplemental material 2 . Selection process Two reviewers (JW and CR) independently searched and extracted citations from each database. All duplicates were removed manually. The same reviewers conducted the selection process independently following title and abstract. Next, selected studies were retrieved and independently assessed based on their full text by the two reviewers to make the final inclusion. Any discrepancies were resolved by discussion between the two assessors. If no agreement was reached, another reviewer (FP) determined whether the article met inclusion criteria or not. We also searched the reference lists at the end of the included studies to identify additional relevant articles. Data collection process Two reviewers (JW and CR) independently extracted information in an excel form regarding: authors, year of publication, study design, number and characteristics of participants, inclusion and exclusion criteria, details of the intervention (immersive or non-immersive) and comparator, outcomes, follow-up times, dropouts and withdrawals. Any disagreements were resolved by a third assessor (FP). The primary outcome was dyspnoea. Secondary outcomes were exercise capacity, muscle function and HRQOL. Data were reported in standardised data recording forms as means±SD. In case of missing data, authors were contacted for clarification. Risk-of-bias appraisal Two assessors (JW and CR) independently evaluated the risk of bias (ROB). For this purpose, the Cochrane risk of bias tool (ROB2) was used. 23 Disagreements between the assessors were resolved by discussion with the methodologist (GC) if consensus was not reached. Statistical analysis As dyspnoea was measured on different scales, standardised mean differences (SMDs) were calculated. 24 For secondary outcomes, MDs were calculated. As we assumed heterogeneity across studies, we used the random-effects model to obtain the summary estimate. Data are presented using a forest plot (point estimates with 95% CIs). Heterogeneity was investigated using forest plot inspection and I² statistic (with I² strictly over 50% considered as substantial). Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore heterogeneity according to: (1) immersive or non-immersive VR, (2) single session or multiple sessions, (3) population (COVID-19, COPD, others) and (4) acute or chronic conditions. A funnel plot was used to assess publication bias and influence analysis was performed by calculating pooled estimates omitting one study at a time. This analysis was performed in the R language environment (V.4.2.2). Full details of statistical analysis are provided in online supplemental material 3 . Two independent reviewers (JW and CR) also assessed for each outcome the certainty of evidence following the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. 25 Patient and public involvement There was no patient or public involvement in the design and conduct of the present study. Results Study selection A total of 6624 records were identified until 17 March 2025. 2914 duplicates were removed before the screening. The remaining 3710 reports were screened for eligibility criteria and 3657 did not meet the inclusion criteria during title and abstract analysis. Handsearching identified seven reports. Next, 60 studies were assessed for eligibility and 45 reports were excluded during this full-text analysis, with the main reason for exclusion being unpublished (n=16) or not being a VR intervention (n=11) (Full details of exclusion in online supplemental material 4 ). Following The Cochrane Handbook, 22 four reports were considered as two studies, with common register numbers NCT05244135 26 27 and ACTRN12617000275369. 28 29 Finally, 15 reports 26 , 40 were included with a total of 13 studies. 2628 30 , 40 Full details of the study selection process are available in figure 1 . Figure 1 PRISMA flow diagram of the study selection process. PRISMA, Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses; VR, virtual reality. Study characteristics Nine of the included studies were classified as randomised controlled trial (RCT). 2628 30 33 35 , 37 39 40 Four studies were classified as cross-over controlled studies. 31 32 34 38 Only one study was multicentre. 35 Total sample size was 483 participants. Most of them had COPD (n=325), 2830 32 , 34 36 37 39 acute COVID-19 (n=44) 35 or post-COVID-19 syndrome (n=52). 26 38 Participants’ ages ranged between 28 and 71 years. As only two studies included participants in acute settings (n=44), 30 35 most of the total size was in stable conditions (n=389). 2628 31 , 34 36 The characteristics of the included studies are synthesised in table 1 ( online supplemental material 5 and table S1 ). Table 1 Characteristics of the included studies Authors, year, country Design Number of participants Respiratory disorders Intervention Outcomes Duration Number of sessions Intervention group Control group Kizmaz et al , 2024, Turkey 30 RCT 50 Acute exacerbation of COPD (hospitalised) N/S 3 Standard rehabilitation+immersive VR Standard rehabilitation MRC 1STS Kuys et al , 2011, Australia 31 Cross over 19 Cystic fibrosis 2 days 1 Non-immersive VR Moderate interval training Borg LeGear et al , 2016, Canada 32 Cross over 10 COPD 1 day 1 Non-immersive VR Continuous moderate training Borg Mazzoleni et al , 2014, Italy 33 RCT 40 Chronic respiratory disease 21 days 21 Standard rehabilitation Non-immersive VR Standard rehabilitation MRC-6MWT-SGRQ Nicolas et al , 2021, France 34 Cross over 20 Chronic respiratory disease 1 day 1 Non-immersive VR Endurance training Borg Rodrigues et al , 2022, Brazil 35 RCT 44 Acute COVID-19 (hospitalised) 1 day 1 Usual therapy+immersive VR Usual therapy+sham immersive VR Numeric Scale Rutkowski et al , 2020, Poland 28 RCT 110 COPD 2 weeks 10 Standard rehabilitation+non immersive VR Standard rehabilitation 6MWT Rutkowski et al , 2021, Poland 36 RCT 50 COPD 2 weeks 10 Standard rehabilitation+immersive VR Standard rehabilitation 6MWT Rutkowski et al , 2023, Poland 26 RCT 32 Post-COVID-19 Syndrome 3 weeks 15 Standard rehabilitation+immersive VR Standard rehabilitation Borg-6MWT- WHOQOL-BREF Simsekli et al , 2025, Turkey 37 RCT 48 COPD 8 weeks 24 Usual care+immersive VR Usual care MRC SGRQ Stavrou et al , 2023, Greece 38 Cross over 20 Post-COVID-19 Syndrome 1 day 1 Cycling with immersive VR Continuous endurance training Borg Sutanto et al , 2019, Indonesia 39 RCT 20 COPD 6 weeks 18 Cycle endurance training+non-immersive VR Cycle endurance training MRC-6MWT-SGRQ Yuen et al , 2019, USA 40 RCT 20 Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis 12 weeks 36 Non-immersive VR Sham non- immersive VR Borg-6MWT SGRQ COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; WHOQOL, WHO Quality of Life. Interventions are synthesised in table 1 ( online supplemental material 5 and table S2 ). Seven studies focused on a non-immersive VR tool. 2831 , 34 39 40 Six studies used an immersive VR tool through VR head-mounted display goggles. 2630 35 , 38 Five studies focused on the immediate impact of the treatment, 31 32 34 35 38 while eight studies investigated a longer-term effect by incorporating the treatment into a rehabilitation programme. 26 28 30 33 36 37 39 40 Only three studies used a relaxation-based rest therapy 35 36 or breathing exercises, 37 while the remaining studies applied an exercise therapy 2830 , 34 38 or a combination of both components. 26 Finally, four studies use VR alone compared with usual care (cycling or exercise training), 31 32 34 38 while the rest of the studies incorporate VR in addition to usual care. 2628 30 33 35 , 37 39 40 Risk of bias For dyspnoea, only one study had an overall low ROB, 40 while the others were considered to have some concerns (n=4) 26 30 35 37 or high ROB (n=3). 33 38 39 Details of bias assessment are available in figure 2 and online supplemental figure S1 . Figure 2 Summary of risk of bias 2. (A) Outcomes on dyspnoea. (B) Outcomes on exercise capacity. (C) Outcomes on HRQOL. *For Stavrou 2023: In bias arising from domain S (Bias arising from period and carryover effects), some concerns were identified. Risk-of-bias plots were created using the Robvis tool (McGuinness, LA, Higgins, JPT. Risk-of-bias VISualization (robvis): An R package and Shiny web app for visualizing risk-of-bias assessments. Res Syn Meth. 2020; 1–7. https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1411 ). HRQOL, Health-related quality of life. Results Dyspnoea Seven RCTs 26 30 33 35 37 39 40 and four cross-over trials 31 32 34 38 compared dyspnoea between VR and standard treatment. Three studies 31 32 34 were not included in the quantitative analysis for several reasons described in the discussion. Finally, eight studies were pooled in the meta-analysis. 2630 33 35 37 , 40 These studies enrolled 273 participants (138 in the control group and 135 in the VR group). Quantitative synthesis showed no difference between groups on dyspnoea (SMD 0.02, 95% CI (−0.82 to 0.86), I 2 =88.2%) with a substantial heterogeneity ( figure 3 and online supplemental figure S2a ). Our certainty was very low because of serious concerns about a high ROB, heterogeneity and imprecision ( online supplemental table S3 ). Figure 3 Meta-analysis of comparative effects between VR and control group on dyspnoea. ( A ) All studies, ( B ) Forest plots of subgroup analyses: single session versus multiple sessions. SMD, standardised mean difference; VR, virtual reality. In subgroup analyses, the number of studies is insufficient in some subgroups and substantial heterogeneity remains in all subgroups ( figure 3 and online supplemental figures S2b, S2c and S2d ). Secondary outcomes: exercise capacity, quality of life and muscle function Seven RCTs compared exercise capacity between VR and standard treatment. 26 28 30 33 36 39 40 Five of these were pooled, 26 28 33 39 40 as they each measured 6 min walk test (6MWT) distance. For the two remaining studies, as the 1 min sit-to-stand 30 and the metabolic equivalent of task 36 have distinct constructs, it prevented us from meta-analysing it with 6MWT. These 5 studies enrolled 183 participants (88 participants in the control group and 95 participants in the VR group). 26 28 33 39 40 Random-effects meta-analysis showed no difference between groups on exercise capacity (MD 3.62, 95% CI (−19.39 to 26.63), I 2 =39.8%) with a moderate heterogeneity ( figure 4A ). The two remaining studies reported little to no difference in favour of VR on exercise capacity. 30 36 Our certainty was low because of serious concerns about imprecision ( online supplemental table S3 ). Figure 4 Meta-analysis of comparative effects between VR and control group on exercise capacity and HRQOL ( A ) Exercise capacity, ( B ) HRQOL. HRQOL, health-related quality of life; MD, mean difference; VR, virtual reality. Five RCTs compared HRQOL between VR and standard treatment. 27 33 37 39 40 Four RCTs were pooled, as they each measured HRQOL using St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ). 33 37 39 40 The remaining study reported HRQOL using the WHO Quality of Life-BREF questionnaire, 27 which has the distinctive characteristic of not having a total score; it prevented us from meta-analysing it with SGRQ. These studies enrolled 127 participants (64 participants in the standard group and 63 participants in the VR group). The pooled results showed no difference between groups on HRQOL (MD −11.81, 95% CI (−42.95 to 19.33), I 2 =98.9%) with a substantial heterogeneity ( figure 4B ). Rutkowski et al reported no difference between groups on HRQOL. 27 Our certainty was very low because of serious concerns about a high ROB, heterogeneity and imprecision ( online supplemental table S3 ). Two RCTs 28 33 and two cross-over trials 34 38 reported outcomes concerning muscle function. This includes quantitative measures such as maximal inspiratory pressure 33 and leg strength, 28 or qualitative measures such as self-reported muscle fatigue 38 or hardship. 34 Lack of data and outcomes’ heterogeneity prevented us from conducting a pooled analysis. Finally, only one study reported adverse effects and indicated that no adverse events were associated with VR. 40 Influence analysis and publication bias assessment are provided in online supplemental material 6 and figures S3a, S3b, S3c . Discussion Summary of main results Thirteen studies were identified in this meta-analysis. 2628 30 , 40 Only two studies were conducted in acute settings. 30 35 The data available were insufficient for the drawing of definitive conclusions regarding muscle function 28 33 34 38 and adverse effects, as only one study reported this latter outcome. 40 Available evidence is very uncertain regarding the impact of VR on dyspnoea and HRQOL on individuals with respiratory disorders suffering from dyspnoea. Furthermore, evidence is unclear as to the effect on exercise capacity, as the CI includes both a clinically important benefit and a potential negative effect. Our results are consistent with two recent meta-analyses, in which no effect of VR on dyspnoea has been demonstrated. 41 42 Compared with the first one, we included more studies and focused on an adult population. 41 Similarly, Patsaki et al pooled two studies to estimate effect on dyspnoea. 42 The authors focused on a specific population (COPD) rather than the symptom, whereas we included all adults with respiratory disease experiencing dyspnoea. Conversely, a recent meta-analysis showed a positive effect on dyspnoea which is inconsistent with our results. In this meta-analysis, the authors combined the COPD Assessment Test (CAT) with mMRC. 20 As mMRC captures activity-related dyspnoea, the CAT measures multiple symptoms such as cough or sleeping. In contrast, our results were obtained by pooling scales that only measured dyspnoea. Moreover, included studies in this meta-analysis are different, which may be attributable to the selection of COPD alone and the use of Chinese databases and studies. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted to explore the high heterogeneity of our results, considering several aspects: (1) immersive and non-immersive modalities, (2) single and multiple exposures, (3) the population of interest and (4) acute or chronic. Immersive and non-immersive modalities Subgroup analysis comparing immersive and non-immersive VR shows considerable imprecision and a high heterogeneity within groups, preventing us from drawing any conclusion. However, the degree of immersion and modalities of VR is a key aspect to be considered. Indeed, the sense of presence grows with the level of immersion, fostering greater user engagement. 17 Consequently, the use of an immersive VR device may be more effective than a non-immersive one in distracting participants, modulating emotional responses and enhancing self-efficacy and motivation. Moreover, a greater level of immersion and engagement may be linked to a greater motivation and satisfaction, thus increasing adherence. 37 43 A suitable design to address these differences would be to compare levels of immersion. Short-term effect (single exposure) Five studies used VR after a single exposure. 31 32 34 35 38 Nonetheless, we included only two studies to assess short-term effects. The remaining three studies were not pooled in the meta-analysis for several reasons. 31 32 34 First, participants had to exercise for a defined period at a fixed target dyspnoea that induced sufficient symptoms, either in the intervention or control groups. 31 32 34 Second, having the same exertional dyspnoea target value in both groups prevents clear interpretation of dyspnoea evolution. Moreover, doing exercises with the aim of reaching a certain level of dyspnoea requires focusing on this symptom, which makes distraction difficult to achieve. Nevertheless, distraction is not the only explanation for how VR works. In studies on pain, full immersion has shown positive results when participants were asked to focus on their pain in order to control it, suggesting a different mechanism from that of simple distraction. 44 A similar effect may be produced by focusing on dyspnoea in specific conditions. However, the use of non-immersive exercise modalities by Kuys et al , 31 LeGear et al 32 and Nicolas et al 34 makes it difficult to draw conclusions, as it is not directly transposable to immersive VR. Conversely, Stavrou et al reported slightly different exercise procedures. 38 Participants were cycling with an immersive VR headset at a constant and defined speed without any consideration about dyspnoea. 38 Unfortunately, despite full immersion, participants experienced mild dyspnoea during the intervention, which did not demonstrate a potential difference in dyspnoea intensity associated with VR use. Greater effort may be necessary to induce sufficient dyspnoea as it is done during pulmonary rehabilitation. 45 Moreover, the duration of exertion may appear to have been insufficient, with a constant exertion period of only 10 min, as supported by the perceived difficulty reported by the participants in this study. Consequently, in order to test the distraction hypothesis, an objective physical exertion target (eg, heart rate, oxygen consumption or work rate) should be set, with the patient being either exposed to VR or not. Long-term effect (repetitive exposure) On the other hand, six studies using VR in repetitive exposure were pooled in our meta-analysis. 26 30 33 37 39 40 Interestingly, whereas 6 weeks of rehabilitation are usually recommended as the optimal duration whether in case of stable chronic diseases (COPD) or postacute conditions such as COVID-19, 11 only two studies had an intervention period and a follow-up superior to 3 weeks. 39 40 Unexpectedly, these two RCTs revealed an effect on dyspnoea favouring control groups. 39 40 However, in the study from Yuen et al , 40 while having the lowest ROB, the adherence rate to VR treatment remains a major issue as only 20% of the participants eventually underwent the intervention. Another confounding factor is the severity at baseline with more severe disease and impairment in VR groups, which has been known as a predictor for a lesser response to rehabilitation. 46 In the study from Sutanto et al , 39 with high ROB, dyspnoea was evaluated by the mMRC score, a tool unable to measure exertional dyspnoea precisely. 47 Dyspnoea assessment Studies included in this systematic review measure dyspnoea with different tools such as mMRC, 30 33 37 39 Baseline Dyspnoea Index (BDI) 33 39 and Borg dyspnoea. 26 31 32 34 38 40 Although these measures are correlated and have enabled us to pool them in our meta-analysis, they capture different dimensions of dyspnoea. The mMRC, which categorises the level of activity-related dyspnoea, reflects the level of exertion at which dyspnoea limits the activity. 48 One limitation of this scale is that it may underestimate dyspnoea in people who actually avoid certain activities to prevent dyspnoea. 47 On the other hand, the Borg dyspnoea scale only captured the intensity-related to a 6MWT. An important limitation of this scale is that it does not assess dyspnoea in relation to a standardised level of exertion (such as a constant workload cycling test). For instance, while the 6MWT is a valid test of exercise capacity, distance may increase with treatment but the level of dyspnoea is likely to be unchanged. 48 Determining a fixed level of exertion thus seems necessary in this context. Finally, mMRC and Borg dyspnoea scales are unidimensional and show clear limitations in measuring changes during interventions for complex dyspnoea-specific phenomena. 47 48 Multidimensional dyspnoea scales may allow for a more accurate analysis. 49 BDI and Transition Dyspnoea Index are of peculiar interest in this context. 33 39 However, despite a better sensitivity to changes, their characteristics did not allow a meta-analysis with other scales. Implications for practice and research Our confidence in effect estimates prevents us from drawing recommendations on the use of VR in clinical practice. Nevertheless, numerous applications of VR are described in this systematic review, providing a comprehensive overview of the current literature in this field. Studies mainly focused on breathing exercises, endurance training, exergaming or promoting relaxation through techniques similar to hypnosis. In pulmonary rehabilitation, VR may promote engagement during cycle endurance training and, in this context, enable a higher level or a higher volume of effort, thus maximising the effectiveness of rehabilitation. 17 Besides distraction, dyspnoea expectation is another important aspect to consider. 50 For instance, Finnegan et al focused on the ‘manipulation of the brain’ through immersive VR: they demonstrated that during a pedalling exercise, immersion in a simulation of varying uphill gradients influenced the perception of dyspnoea independently of the workload. 16 This is an interesting finding that could be applied in respiratory rehabilitation, where participants may experience anxious anticipation or fear of dyspnoea. 50 Moreover, through safe, repeated and graded exposure to dyspnoea, VR could have positive effects on the fear of dyspnoea, similar to its impact on kinesiophobia in chronic pain 44 None of the included studies considered breathing patterns during physical activities. However, people with COPD may experience dynamic hyperinflation during exercise. 51 Managing respiratory rate and hyperinflation during exertion is thus crucial as it could increase exercise tolerance. 52 Interestingly, in passive conditions without exercises, participants receiving VR in addition to synchronous feedback of their breathing, embodied via a virtual body, improved their dyspnoea in comparison to those receiving asynchronous feedback under VR. 14 Finally, traditional rehabilitation conducted at a centre has several limits which hinder the completion of sessions. Şimşekli and Tan have focused on performing home-based breathing exercises with immersive VR, such as pursed lips and diaphragmatic breathing. 37 Interestingly, this study demonstrated the most positive effects with a great satisfaction according to the participants and a high adherence. Conversely, Yuen et al reported a poor adherence in their home-based rehabilitation. 40 Participants in this study were instructed to ‘play’ with a non-immersive VR without supervision. The supervision approach used by Şimşekli and Tan could explain the positive result. 37 Beyond the potential impact of varying degrees of immersion, this is an innovative and unfamiliar tool for some people. Monitoring seems essential in this context to ensure proper use and safety. This is particularly relevant as one of the major advantages of VR is its potential for adaptation on a tailored basis. Limitations and strengths This study has some limitations. First, participants included in this meta-analysis mostly suffered from COPD and COVID-19, limiting the external validity in other chronic respiratory diseases. Nonetheless, this strengthens the level of evidence for these two pathologies. Second, despite heterogeneity in intervention, duration of session and follow-up, number of sessions and exercise intensity, these broad treatment modalities suggest numerous applications of VR. Third, the inability to conduct a meta-analysis on changes from baseline may potentially reduce the power of the analysis by failing to account for baseline imbalances for small-sample trials. However, this highlights the importance of ensuring that new studies report their findings adequately or in sharing individual-level data in repositories. Fourth, beyond a seemingly modest sample size, it appears important to note that VR is a recent therapy, and several RCTs have been identified as actively recruiting and not yet published. Our study has some strengths. The broad database screening allowed us to explore a large number of studies. Moreover, the inclusion of recent studies provides an update of pre-existing systematic reviews. Finally, this meta-analysis highlights the need to address several gaps in studies using VR: (1) few studies were conducted in acute settings, (2) data are scarce regarding muscle function, (3) proper designs are required to assess effects in single exposure and short-term effects, (4) many applications are possible in regard to the different objectives: distraction, treating dyspnoea expectation or fear of dyspnoea, being more engaging and enjoyable, (5) more appropriate dyspnoea tools, such as multidimensional scales, are highly relevant in this context and (6) adverse events are not systematically reported. Future studies should exercise the utmost vigilance on this particular matter and ensure that adverse events, such as cybersickness, 53 are reported in a clear and unambiguous manner. Conclusions This meta-analysis found that available evidence is very uncertain regarding the impact of VR on dyspnoea and HRQOL in adults with respiratory diseases. Furthermore, evidence is unclear as to the effect on exercise capacity. VR opens new perspectives and further studies with proper methodological designs and more appropriate dyspnoea assessments are needed to demonstrate the potential effects of VR on individuals with respiratory disorders suffering from dyspnoea. Moreover, few studies have investigated the impact of such interventions on muscle function, despite its major role in rehabilitation. documents.title: Effectiveness of Digital Health Interventions for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), marked by dyspnea, cough, and sputum production, significantly impairs patients' quality of life and functionality. Effective management strategies, particularly those empowering patients to manage their condition, are essential to reduce this burden and health care use. Digital health interventions-such as mobile apps for symptom tracking, wearable sensors for vital sign monitoring, and web-based pulmonary rehabilitation programs-can enhance self-efficacy and promote greater patient engagement. By improving self-management skills, these interventions also help alleviate pressure on health care systems.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis assesses the clinical effectiveness of smartphone apps, wearable monitors, and web-delivered platforms in four COPD management areas: (1) quality of life (measured by the COPD Assessment Test [CAT] and St George's Respiratory Questionnaire), (2) self-efficacy (assessed by the General Self-Efficacy Scale), (3) functional capacity (evaluated via the 6-minute walk test and Modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale), and (4) health care use (indicated by hospital and emergency department visits).
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted using predefined search terms in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and Web of Science up to January 26, 2025, to identify randomized trials on digital health interventions for COPD. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Outcomes included quality of life, self-efficacy, functional status, and health care use.
RESULTS: This review included 17 studies with 2027 participants from 11 countries. Eleven trials involved health care professionals in digital platform use, and 12 reported adherence strategies. Digital tools for COPD primarily focused on telerehabilitation (eg, video-guided exercises) and self-management systems (eg, artificial intelligence-driven exacerbation alerts). The study participants were predominantly older adults. Meta-analysis results indicated that digital health interventions significantly improved quality of life at 3 months on the CAT (mean difference [MD] -1.65, 95% CI -3.17 to -0.14; P=.03); at 6 months on the CAT (MD -2.43, 95% CI -3.93 to -0.94; P=.001) and St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (MD 3.25, 95% CI 0.69-5.81; P=.01); at 12 months on the CAT (MD -2.53, 95% CI -3.91 to -1.16; P<.001), EQ-5D (MD 0.04, 95% CI 0.01-0.07; P=.02), and EQ-5D visual analogue scale (MD 5.88, 95% CI 0.38-11.37; P=.04); the General Self-Efficacy Scale at 3 months (MD 1.65, 95% CI 0.62-2.69; P=.002) and 6 months (MD 1.94, 95% CI 0.83-3.05; P<.001); and the Modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale at more than 3 months (MD -0.23, 95% CI -0.36 to -0.11; P=.003). However, no significant differences were observed in the 6-minute walk test, emergency department admissions, hospital admissions, emergency department admissions for COPD, or hospital admissions for COPD.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that digital health interventions may benefit COPD patients, but their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain. Further robust studies are needed, particularly those involving larger numbers of older adults with COPD.

Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), marked by dyspnea, cough, and sputum production, significantly impairs patients’ quality of life and functionality. Effective management strategies, particularly those empowering patients to manage their condition, are essential to reduce this burden and health care use. Digital health interventions—such as mobile apps for symptom tracking, wearable sensors for vital sign monitoring, and web-based pulmonary rehabilitation programs—can enhance self-efficacy and promote greater patient engagement. By improving self-management skills, these interventions also help alleviate pressure on health care systems. Objective This systematic review and meta-analysis assesses the clinical effectiveness of smartphone apps, wearable monitors, and web-delivered platforms in four COPD management areas: (1) quality of life (measured by the COPD Assessment Test [CAT] and St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire), (2) self-efficacy (assessed by the General Self-Efficacy Scale), (3) functional capacity (evaluated via the 6-minute walk test and Modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale), and (4) health care use (indicated by hospital and emergency department visits). Methods A systematic review was conducted using predefined search terms in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and Web of Science up to January 26, 2025, to identify randomized trials on digital health interventions for COPD. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Outcomes included quality of life, self-efficacy, functional status, and health care use. Results This review included 17 studies with 2027 participants from 11 countries. Eleven trials involved health care professionals in digital platform use, and 12 reported adherence strategies. Digital tools for COPD primarily focused on telerehabilitation (eg, video-guided exercises) and self-management systems (eg, artificial intelligence–driven exacerbation alerts). The study participants were predominantly older adults. Meta-analysis results indicated that digital health interventions significantly improved quality of life at 3 months on the CAT (mean difference [MD] −1.65, 95% CI –3.17 to –0.14; P =.03); at 6 months on the CAT (MD −2.43, 95% CI −3.93 to −0.94; P =.001) and St George’s Respiratory Questionnaire (MD 3.25, 95% CI 0.69-5.81; P =.01); at 12 months on the CAT (MD −2.53, 95% CI −3.91 to −1.16; P <.001), EQ-5D (MD 0.04, 95% CI 0.01-0.07; P =.02), and EQ-5D visual analogue scale (MD 5.88, 95% CI 0.38-11.37; P =.04); the General Self-Efficacy Scale at 3 months (MD 1.65, 95% CI 0.62-2.69; P =.002) and 6 months (MD 1.94, 95% CI 0.83-3.05; P <.001); and the Modified Medical Research Council Dyspnea Scale at more than 3 months (MD −0.23, 95% CI −0.36 to −0.11; P =.003). However, no significant differences were observed in the 6-minute walk test, emergency department admissions, hospital admissions, emergency department admissions for COPD, or hospital admissions for COPD. Conclusions Our findings suggest that digital health interventions may benefit COPD patients, but their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain. Further robust studies are needed, particularly those involving larger numbers of older adults with COPD.
